# 2026-11-21: How information about the contact propagates through the body {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** exploratory · **Thread:** T2 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_propagation.py`
:::

**Question.** @sec-langevin found that, in a body thermalized by its own dampers, every
design holds the same information about the contact force, and designs differ in how much
of it a given part of the body holds. What decides how much reaches a part, and what
erodes it on the way?

**Short answer.** A part of the body holds the contact force as if the contact damping
were larger than it is: it sees the force through an *effective contact damping*
$b_{\rm eff}(\omega)\ge b_c$. The ratio $\rho(\omega)=b_c/b_{\rm eff}(\omega)$, between 0 and
1, is the fraction that propagates to the part at frequency $\omega$. It falls below 1 for
one reason only: thermal noise from dampers inside the body that the force has to cross
on its way to the part. Inertia and compliance matter through how they shape that noise
at the part. With no internal damper, every part holds everything. On the SEA at
$k_s=70$ the joint-side link holds 98% of the body's information and the rotor, behind
the series damper, holds 6%.

## Setting and definitions

Take the Langevin body of @sec-langevin: thermal forces with covariance $2\sigma_T^2D$,
started from the Gibbs law. Split the damping into the contact damper and everything else,
$$
D=b_c\,J^\top J+D_{\rm int},\qquad D_{\rm int}\succeq0 .
$$
For the legs in this book $b_c=b_i=600$ N s/m. For the rigid leg $D_{\rm int}=0$. For the
SEA, $D_{\rm int}$ is the series damper $b_s$ acting on the spring deflection.

A *part* of the body is a set of its coordinates, $x_P=Px_q$ for a selector matrix $P$. The
rotor's angle and velocity form one part; the joint-side link's angle and velocity form
another. Nothing is added to $x_P$: the only noise is the body's own.

::: {#def-share name="Information share"}
For a force profile acting over a window, the *share* of a part $P$ is
$$
\eta_P=\frac{I(w;\,x_P)}{I(w;\,x_q)},
$$
the information held by the part's trajectory divided by the information held by the
whole body's.
:::

::: {#def-beff name="Effective contact damping"}
At frequency $\omega$, let $h(\omega)=P(i\omega-A)^{-1}B_F$ be the part's response to the
contact force and $G(\omega)=P(i\omega-A)^{-1}[0;H^{-1}]$ its response to a generalized
force. Let
$$
M(\omega)=2\sigma_T^2\,G\,D_{\rm int}\,G^*
$$
be the thermal noise the part receives from the internal dampers, and
$q(\omega)=h^*M^+h$, with $q=\infty$ when $h$ lies outside the range of $M$. The
*effective contact damping* is
$$
b_{\rm eff}(\omega)=b_c+\frac{1}{2\sigma_T^2\,q(\omega)},
$$
and the *spectral share* is $\rho(\omega)=b_c/b_{\rm eff}(\omega)$.
:::

## Results

::: {#prp-share-basic name="Bounds and invariances"}

(a) $0\le\eta_P\le1$ and $0\le\rho(\omega)\le1$.
(b) A part that contains another holds at least as much: adding rows to $P$ cannot lower
    $\eta_P$ or $\rho(\omega)$.
(c) $\eta_P$ and $\rho$ belong to the physical part, not to the coordinates: under
    $q=T\tilde q$ the same part has selector $P\mathcal T$, and both quantities are
    unchanged.
(d) $\rho$ depends on the part only through the row space of $P$, and not on $\sigma_T$ or
    on the force prior.
(e) A coordinate alone and the coordinate with its velocity have the same $\rho$.
:::

::: {.proof}
(a) The part is a function of the whole state, so data processing gives
$I(w;x_P)\le I(w;x_q)$. For $\rho$: $q\ge0$ because $M\succeq0$, so $b_{\rm eff}\ge b_c$.

(b) A larger part contains the smaller one's trajectory, so data processing again gives
the inequality for $\eta$. For $\rho$, appending rows to $P$ can only increase $h^*M^+h$,
the signal-to-noise ratio of the best linear combination of the rows.

(c) Under $q=T\tilde q$ the trajectories and the thermal forces are the same physical
signals written in other coordinates (@thm-invariance), so every information quantity
is unchanged. The transfer functions $h$ and $G\,D_{\rm int}G^*$ are unchanged for the
same reason.

(d) Replacing $P$ by $SP$ with $S$ invertible maps $h\mapsto Sh$ and $M\mapsto SMS^*$, which
leaves $h^*M^+h$ unchanged. $M$ is proportional to $\sigma_T^2$, so $\sigma_T^2q$ and
hence $b_{\rm eff}$ do not depend on $\sigma_T$. The prior does not appear at all.

(e) In the frequency domain a velocity is $i\omega$ times its coordinate, so the part
(coordinate, velocity) has $h=v\,h_\theta$ and $M=v\,M_\theta\,v^*$ with $v=(1,i\omega)^\top$.
Then $M^+=v v^*/(M_\theta|v|^4)$, and $h^*M^+h=|h_\theta|^2/M_\theta$, the value for the
coordinate alone. Thermal noise moves the velocity and the coordinate together, so the
velocity adds no independent look at the force.
:::

::: {#thm-beff name="A part holds the force through an effective damper"}
In the stationary, infinite-window limit, with force spectrum $S(\omega)$, the
information rate held by the part is
$$
\dot I_P=\int_0^{\infty}\log\Big(1+\frac{S(\omega)}{2\sigma_T^2\,b_{\rm eff}(\omega)}\Big)\,
\frac{d\omega}{2\pi}\ \text{nats/s},
$$
and the whole body's rate is the same expression with $b_{\rm eff}=b_c$.
:::

::: {.proof}
*Step 1: the contact damper's noise enters like the force.* The thermal forces have
covariance $2\sigma_T^2D=2\sigma_T^2(b_cJ^\top J+D_{\rm int})$. In law they equal
$J^\top\xi_c+\xi_{\rm int}$, with $\xi_c$ a scalar white noise of intensity $2\sigma_T^2b_c$
and $\xi_{\rm int}$ an independent white noise of covariance $2\sigma_T^2D_{\rm int}$.
Since $f$ also enters through $J^\top$, the part's trajectory is
$$
x_P=h\,(f+\xi_c)+G\,\xi_{\rm int} .
$$

*Step 2: one frequency.* At each frequency this is a scalar Gaussian signal $f$ in
Gaussian noise of spectral density $N=2\sigma_T^2b_c\,hh^*+M$. The information rate of a
stationary Gaussian signal in independent stationary Gaussian noise is the integral of
$\log(1+S\,h^*N^{-1}h)$ over frequency [@cover2006elements, Ch. 9].

*Step 3: Sherman-Morrison.* With $u=\sqrt{2\sigma_T^2b_c}\,h$,
$(M+uu^*)^{-1}=M^{-1}-M^{-1}uu^*M^{-1}/(1+u^*M^{-1}u)$, so
$$
h^*N^{-1}h=\frac{q}{1+2\sigma_T^2b_c\,q}=\frac{1}{2\sigma_T^2b_c+1/q}
=\frac{1}{2\sigma_T^2b_{\rm eff}} .
$$
When $M$ is singular the same holds with $M^+$, and $q=\infty$ gives $b_{\rm eff}=b_c$.

*Step 4: the whole body.* With $P=I$, $h=G\,J^\top$ and $M=2\sigma_T^2GD_{\rm int}G^*$. The
matrix $G=(i\omega-A)^{-1}[0;H^{-1}]$ has full column rank, so $h$ lies in the range of
$M$ exactly when $J^\top$ lies in the range of $D_{\rm int}$. For the rigid leg
$D_{\rm int}=0$. For the SEA its range is spanned by $(1,-1)$, which does not contain
$J^\top=(-r,0)$. So $q=\infty$ and $b_{\rm eff}=b_c$, consistent with @prp-contact.
:::

::: {#cor-lossless name="No internal damper, no loss"}
If the only damper is at the contact ($D_{\rm int}=0$) and $h(\omega)\ne0$ over the force
band, then $\rho\equiv1$: *every* part holds everything the body holds. In the rigid leg
the rotor's angle alone holds the full ceiling, and so does its velocity alone.
:::

::: {.proof}
$M=0$, so $h$ lies outside the range of $M$ wherever $h\ne0$, and $b_{\rm eff}=b_c$.
:::

::: {#prp-sea-parts name="The SEA's rotor and link"}
For the clamped SEA with series damping $b_s=2\zeta_s\sqrt{k_sI_{\rm rot}}$,
$m_j=m_lr^2$ and $c=k_s+ib_s\omega$,
$$
\rho_{\rm rotor}=\Big[1+\frac{b_s}{b_c}\,
\frac{|k_ir^2-m_j\omega^2+i\omega b_cr^2|^2}{r^2|c|^2}\Big]^{-1},\qquad
\rho_{\rm link}=\Big[1+\frac{b_s}{b_c}\,
\frac{I_{\rm rot}^2\omega^4}{r^2|c-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2|^2}\Big]^{-1}.
$$
:::

::: {.proof}
By @prp-share-basic(e) it is enough to work with each part's angle.

*Step 1: the impedance matrix.* With $z_g=k_ir^2+i\omega b_cr^2-m_j\omega^2$ the
joint-side impedance, the clamped equations read $Z q=J^\top f+\dots$ with
$Z=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}z_g+c&-c\\-c&-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2+c\end{smallmatrix}\right]$ and
$\Delta=\det Z$, so
$Z^{-1}=\Delta^{-1}\left[\begin{smallmatrix}-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2+c&c\\c&z_g+c
\end{smallmatrix}\right]$.

*Step 2: the two inputs.* The contact force enters as $J^\top=(-r,0)$. The series damper
acts on the deflection, so its noise enters as $a_s=(1,-1)$ with intensity
$2\sigma_T^2b_s$.

*Step 3: the rotor* is row 2 of $Z^{-1}$: $h=-rc/\Delta$ and
$h_s=(c-z_g-c)/\Delta=-z_g/\Delta$. With one coordinate,
$1/(2\sigma_T^2q)=b_s|h_s|^2/|h|^2=b_s|z_g|^2/(r^2|c|^2)$.

*Step 4: the link* is row 1: $h=-r(c-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2)/\Delta$ and
$h_s=(c-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2-c)/\Delta=-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2/\Delta$, which gives
$b_s|h_s|^2/|h|^2=b_sI_{\rm rot}^2\omega^4/(r^2|c-I_{\rm rot}\omega^2|^2)$.
:::

The two formulas say where the series damper's noise lands. The rotor sits behind the
damper, so it receives the damper's noise against the force filtered through the spring,
and a soft spring makes that filter weak. The link sits on the contact side. Its losses
come only near the rotor resonance $\sqrt{k_s/I_{\rm rot}}$, where the rotor swings and
pumps the damper's noise back through the spring.

::: {#prp-lowsnr name="At low SNR, the share is the band average of rho"}
With a flat force spectrum over $[0,B]$ and whole-body SNR $\mathrm{snr}=S/(2\sigma_T^2b_c)$,
the infinite-window share is
$\eta=\int_0^B\log(1+\mathrm{snr}\,\rho)\,df\big/\big(B\log(1+\mathrm{snr})\big)$, and
$\eta\to\frac1B\int_0^B\rho\,df$ as $\mathrm{snr}\to0$.
:::

::: {.proof}
The formula for $\eta$ is @thm-beff divided by its whole-body value. As
$\mathrm{snr}\to0$, $\log(1+\mathrm{snr}\,\rho)/\log(1+\mathrm{snr})\to\rho$ for each $f$,
and the ratio is bounded by 1, so the limit passes inside the integral (dominated
convergence).
:::

So $\rho(\omega)$ describes the body and the part without reference to a noise level or
a force prior, and $\eta$ is that description at a stated SNR. A larger SNR compresses the
losses, because the logarithm saturates.

## Numbers

```{python}
#| label: fig-propagation
#| fig-cap: |
#|   (a) Spectral share of the SEA's rotor (solid) and joint-side link (dashed), from the
#|   closed forms of @prp-sea-parts. The link holds almost everything except near the rotor
#|   resonance $\sqrt{k_s/I_{\rm rot}}$; with a soft spring the rotor loses most of the force
#|   to the series damper's noise. (b) Finite-window share $\eta$ against $k_s$, with the
#|   infinite-window prediction of @prp-lowsnr at the book's SNR (dotted).
from mibook import figures
figures.fig_propagation();
```

| $k_s$ (N m/rad) | rotor, finite | rotor, predicted | link, finite | link, predicted |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 70 | 0.060 | 0.068 | 0.984 | 0.985 |
| $10^3$ | 0.494 | 0.518 | 0.907 | 0.910 |
| $10^4$ | 0.930 | 0.951 | 0.986 | 0.994 |
| $10^6$ | 0.995 | 1.000 | 0.998 | 1.000 |

: Share of the body's information held by the SEA's rotor and link, each taken as angle and velocity ($B_w=100$ Hz, $\mathrm{snr}=20.8$). The rigid leg's rotor holds 0.9987 in the finite window and exactly 1 in the prediction. {#tbl-propagation-note}

- The state-space computation and the closed forms agree to $7\times10^{-16}$, and $\rho$
  is unchanged, to $4\times10^{-16}$, under every reparametrization of @fig-invariance
  (`check_closed_forms`, `check_reparametrization`).
- The finite-window share sits up to 0.025 below the prediction. The gap comes from the
  window's edges and from the Gibbs initial state, and shrinks as $k_s$ grows
  (`check_prediction`).
- Series damping is the loss. At $k_s=70$, lowering $\zeta_s$ from 0.1 to 0.03 to 0.01
  raises the rotor's share from 0.060 to 0.095 to 0.200, while the whole body stays at
  37.742 bits (`check_series_damping`).
- At low SNR the share tends to the band average of $\rho$: 0.221 for the rotor at
  $k_s=10^3$, against 0.518 at the book's SNR (`check_low_snr_limit`).

## What this changes

@sec-langevin reported that the share held by the SEA's rotor climbs from 6% to 99.5%
with stiffness. The link of the same SEA holds 91% to 99.8% at every stiffness tested
(@fig-propagation(b)). Where the information sits in the body is decided by where the
internal dampers sit: a part on the contact side of the dissipation holds the force, and
a part behind it holds what survives the damper's thermal noise. Compliance changes this
only through how it filters the force and that noise on the way to each part.

## Limits of this note

- The bench is passive and clamped, with the motor undriven. A part here is a set of the
  body's own coordinates. How a controller or a sensor would use a part is outside the
  scope of this note.
- Damping is viscous and constant.
- The rate formula in @thm-beff is the standard infinite-window result. The finite-window
  numbers are computed directly and agree with it to within 0.025.
